chief_complaint: extreme muscle soreness and dark tea-colored urine after ultramarathon
hpi_details: 31M post-marathon presenting with severe myalgia, dark brown urine (myoglobinuria), CK >40,000 U/L, hyperkalemia, and acute renal failure.
ideas: He thinks he became severely dehydrated during the ultramarathon and that the intense physical jarring bruised his bladder or kidneys.
concerns: He is worried that he has caused permanent damage to his kidneys that will prevent him from ever running competitively again.
expectations: He hopes to receive an intravenous fluid drip to flush out his kidneys and a doctor's note excusing him from work for a couple of days.

investigation_events.title: STAT 12-lead ECG
investigation_events.availability_message: The STAT ECG is now available; IV calcium and hyperkalemia treatment should not be delayed.

results.value: Tall peaked T waves without QRS widening or sine-wave morphology

clinical_knowledge.topic: Rhabdomyolysis with Acute Kidney Injury evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Rhabdomyolysis with Acute Kidney Injury is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes aggressive IV isotonic saline hydration to prevent myoglobin cast formation in renal tubules, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: extreme muscle soreness and dark tea-colored urine after ultramarathon
Key HPI features: 31M post-marathon presenting with severe myalgia, dark brown urine (myoglobinuria), CK >40,000 U/L, hyperkalemia, and acute renal failure.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 108/68, HR 102, Temp 37.8C. Diffuse severe tenderness and mild swelling of bilateral thighs and calves; decreased urine output. Urinalysis: dipstick strongly positive for blood but few/no RBCs on microscopy (myoglobinuria). Bloods: CK 42,000 U/L, Creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), K+ 6.2 mEq/L, Phosphate 5.8 mg/dL, Calcium 7.6 mg/dL, Uric acid elevated. ECG shows peaked T waves.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Rhabdomyolysis with Acute Kidney Injury.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Hemolysis (also causes dark urine, but different lab picture) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Palpitations or muscle weakness — suggests dangerous hyperkalemia from muscle breakdown.
management_principles: Aggressive IV isotonic saline hydration (target urine output >200-300 mL/hr) to prevent myoglobin cast formation in renal tubules
Treat hyperkalemia emergently given K+ 6.2 mEq/L: IV calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, and consider hemodialysis if refractory or ECG worsens
Monitor serial CK, creatinine, and electrolytes (K+, phosphate, calcium) every 6-12 hours
Avoid nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, IV contrast) until renal function recovers
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 31M presents after completing an ultramarathon with severe bilateral leg myalgia and dark tea-colored urine beginning several hours after the race.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 108/68, HR 102, Temp 37.8C. Diffuse severe tenderness and mild swelling of bilateral thighs and calves; decreased urine output. Urinalysis: dipstick strongly positive for blood but few/no RBCs on microscopy (myoglobinuria). Bloods: CK 42,000 U/L, Creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), K+ 6.2 mEq/L, Phosphate 5.8 mg/dL, Calcium 7.6 mg/dL, Uric acid elevated. ECG shows peaked T waves.
reference_soap.assessment: Rhabdomyolysis with Acute Kidney Injury (myoglobin cast nephropathy) secondary to extreme exertion.
reference_soap.plan: Aggressive IV isotonic saline hydration (target urine output >200-300 mL/hr) to prevent myoglobin cast formation in renal tubules. Treat hyperkalemia emergently given K+ 6.2 mEq/L: IV calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, and consider hemodialysis if refractory or ECG worsens. Monitor serial CK, creatinine, and electrolytes every 6-12 hours. Avoid nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, IV contrast) until renal function recovers.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Rhabdomyolysis Acute Kidney Injury
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for extreme muscle soreness and dark tea-colored urine after ultramarathon
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for nephrology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: Extreme muscle breakdown — here from an ultramarathon — releases myoglobin into the blood, which is directly toxic to kidney tubules, causing dark tea-colored urine and a markedly elevated CK.
differentials: Hemolysis (also causes dark urine, but different lab picture)
red_flags: Palpitations or muscle weakness — suggests dangerous hyperkalemia from muscle breakdown

must_ask.say: What kind of intense exercise did you do recently — how long or far?
How severe is the muscle soreness compared to normal post-exercise soreness?
What color is your urine — dark brown or tea-colored?
How much fluid were you drinking during the event?
Any muscle weakness, cramps, or heart palpitations?

history.answer: I ran an ultramarathon yesterday, and since this morning my legs are agonizingly sore and my urine looks like dark black tea.
The dark urine started about four hours after I finished the race yesterday evening, and it has stayed dark brown ever since. I have never had anything like this happen before.
It looks like strong black tea or dark cola, completely brown. I haven't seen any red blood clots in it.
The color is dark throughout the whole stream from start to finish.
No, it doesn't burn or hurt when the urine actually comes out. The only pain I have is the terrible aching in my leg muscles.
It's a ten out of ten deep, throbbing soreness across both my thighs and calves. It hurts even when I'm just lying still, and walking is nearly impossible.
No, I don't have any sharp flank pain or pain shooting down into my groin.
No, I haven't felt an urge to run to the bathroom frequently, and there is no sudden urgency.
I don't have trouble starting to pee, but the stream is quite weak and very little comes out.
Yes, I have barely urinated twice today, just a tiny amount each time. I haven't noticed any foam or froth in it.
My thighs and calves feel swollen and tight, but my face and eyelids aren't puffy at all.
I've felt warm and flushed since finishing the race, but I haven't had shaking chills.
No, I haven't had a sore throat, runny nose, or any skin sores in the past few weeks.
No rash, no joint swelling or stiffness, and I haven't been coughing up any blood.
No unintended weight loss, but I feel completely exhausted and drained.
No nosebleeds, no bleeding from my gums, and I don't bruise easily.
I ran a fifty-mile ultramarathon yesterday in hot weather and pushed myself harder than ever before. I didn't suffer any falls, crashes, or direct blows to my body.
I tried to drink water at the aid stations, but by mile thirty I was vomiting and couldn't keep much down, so I became severely dehydrated.
No, I haven't eaten beets, blackberries, or anything dyed red, and I haven't taken rifampin.
I did feel a slight fluttering in my chest earlier this morning, though it didn't last very long.
My legs feel very weak and heavy, almost giving out when I try to stand, but I don't have numbness or tingling.
No, I don't take aspirin, warfarin, or any blood thinners, and I avoided taking painkillers before or during the race.
I have always been healthy and have no chronic medical conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, or bodybuilding supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink one or two beers socially on weekends, and I didn't drink any alcohol this past week.
I work as an office manager and live with my partner in an apartment. I don't work around dyes, chemicals, or rubber.
There is no family history of kidney disease, kidney failure, or kidney stones.

I figured I was just completely dehydrated from the race and that all the jarring impact over fifty miles bruised my bladder. I'm really worried that I've permanently damaged my kidneys and won't ever be allowed to train or run marathons again.

exam.finding: The patient looks visibly exhausted and uncomfortable due to leg pain, but is alert and conversational.
Blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, pulse 102 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 37.8°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
No periorbital puffiness, conjunctival pallor, or scleral icterus.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal heart sounds; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Clear vesicular breath sounds throughout both lung fields without crackles or wheezes.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended; no palpable masses and the bladder is not distended.
No tenderness elicited over either costovertebral angle.
Mild visible fullness and severe, diffuse tenderness to palpation across both thighs and calves.
Mild muscular swelling over the lower extremities, but no pitting edema at the pretibial areas or ankles.
No petechiae, ecchymoses, track marks, or rashes noted on exposed skin.
Normal sphincter tone with a smooth, non-tender, normal-sized prostate.
